{{Short description|Map from the normal invariants to the L-groups}}
In [[mathematics]], specifically in [[surgery theory]], the '''surgery obstructions''' define a map <math>\theta \colon \mathcal{N} (X) \to L_n (\pi_1 (X))</math> from the [[normal invariant]]s to the [[L-theory|L-group]]s which is in the first instance a set-theoretic map (that means not necessarily a [[homomorphism]]) with the following property when <math>n \geq 5</math>:

A degree-one normal map <math>(f,b) \colon M \to X</math> is normally [[cobordant]] to a [[homotopy equivalence]] if and only if the image <math>\theta (f,b)=0</math> in <math>L_n (\mathbb{Z} [\pi_1 (X)])</math>.

==Sketch of the definition==

The surgery obstruction of a degree-one normal map has a relatively complicated definition.

Consider a degree-one normal map <math>(f,b) \colon M \to X</math>. The idea in deciding the question whether it is normally cobordant to a homotopy equivalence is to try to systematically improve <math>(f,b)</math> so that the map <math>f</math> becomes <math>m</math>-connected (that means the homotopy groups <math>\pi_* (f)=0</math> for <math>* \leq m</math>) for high <math>m</math>. It is a consequence of [[Poincaré duality]] that if we can achieve this for <math>m > \lfloor n/2 \rfloor</math> then the map <math>f</math> already is a homotopy equivalence. The word ''systematically'' above refers to the fact that one tries to do surgeries on <math>M</math> to kill elements of <math>\pi_i (f)</math>. In fact it is more convenient to use [[homology (mathematics)|homology]] of the [[universal cover]]s to observe how connected the map <math>f</math> is. More precisely, one works with the '''surgery kernels''' <math>K_i (\tilde M) : = \mathrm{ker} \{f_* \colon H_i (\tilde M) \rightarrow H_i (\tilde X)\}</math> which one views as <math>\mathbb{Z}[\pi_1 (X)]</math>-modules. If all these vanish, then the map <math>f</math> is a homotopy equivalence. As a consequence of Poincaré duality on <math>M</math> and <math>X</math> there is a <math>\mathbb{Z}[\pi_1 (X)]</math>-modules Poincaré duality <math>K^{n-i} (\tilde M) \cong K_i (\tilde M)</math>, so one only has to watch half of them, that means those for which <math>i \leq \lfloor n/2 \rfloor</math>.

Any degree-one normal map can be made <math>\lfloor n/2 \rfloor</math>-connected by the process called surgery below the middle dimension. This is the process of killing elements of <math>K_i (\tilde M)</math> for <math>i < \lfloor n/2 \rfloor</math> described [[Surgery theory|here]] when we have <math>p+q = n</math> such that <math>i = p < \lfloor n/2 \rfloor</math>. After this is done there are two cases.

1. If <math>n=2k</math> then the only nontrivial homology group is the kernel <math>K_k (\tilde M) : = \mathrm{ker} \{f_* \colon H_k (\tilde M) \rightarrow H_k (\tilde X)\}</math>. It turns out that the cup-product pairings on <math>M</math> and <math>X</math> induce a cup-product pairing on <math>K_k(\tilde M)</math>. This defines a [[symmetric bilinear form]] in case <math>k=2l</math> and a skew-symmetric bilinear form in case <math>k=2l+1</math>. It turns out that these forms can be refined to <math>\varepsilon</math>-quadratic forms, where <math>\varepsilon = (-1)^k</math>. These <math>\varepsilon</math>-quadratic forms define elements in the L-groups <math>L_n (\pi_1 (X))</math>.

2. If <math>n=2k+1</math> the definition is more complicated. Instead of a [[quadratic form]] one obtains from the geometry a quadratic formation, which is a kind of automorphism of quadratic forms. Such a thing defines an element in the odd-dimensional L-group <math>L_n (\pi_1 (X))</math>.

If the element <math>\theta (f,b)</math> is zero in the L-group surgery can be done on <math>M</math> to modify <math>f</math> to a homotopy equivalence.

Geometrically the reason why this is not always possible is that performing surgery in the middle dimension to kill an element in <math>K_k (\tilde M)</math> possibly creates an element in <math>K_{k-1} (\tilde M)</math> when <math>n = 2k</math> or in <math>K_{k} (\tilde M)</math> when <math>n=2k+1</math>. So this possibly destroys what has already been achieved. However, if <math>\theta (f,b)</math> is zero, surgeries can be arranged in such a way that this does not happen.

==Example==

In the simply connected case the following happens.

If <math>n = 2k+1</math> there is no obstruction.

If <math>n = 4l</math> then the surgery obstruction can be calculated as the difference of the signatures of M and X.

If <math>n = 4l+2</math> then the surgery obstruction is the Arf-invariant of the associated kernel quadratic form over <math>\mathbb{Z}_2</math>.
